Here are the verse‑by‑verse notes for **Deuteronomy 9**, drawn from the sites you specified. Where the site’s provenance matters, I have noted the tradition.

---

## Overview

Moses’ aim in this chapter is to demolish any notion that Israel will possess Canaan because of their own righteousness. The chapter falls into three movements: (1) God’s promise of victory (vv. 1‑3), (2) the true reasons for the conquest — Canaanite wickedness and the patriarchal promise, not Israel’s merit (vv. 4‑6), and (3) a lengthy reminder of Israel’s record of rebellion, climaxing in the golden‑calf incident and Moses’ intercession (vv. 7‑29).  
— Matthew Henry (via Precept Austin), https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-9-commentary  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html

---

## v. 1 — “Hear, O Israel: Today you are about to cross the Jordan … nations greater and stronger than you, with large cities fortified to the heavens.”

**Traditional reading:** “Today” (or “this day”) does not mean that very calendar day; the crossing of the Jordan was still about two months away (Joshua 4:19). The expression conveys the imminence and certainty of the event. God does not give Israel false confidence; He realistically describes enemies that are humanly insurmountable so that they will be compelled to radical trust.  
— Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Ellicott: “Thou art passing: i.e., just about to pass,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Enduring Word (Guzik, charismatic), https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

“Cities great and fortified up to heaven” is the same report the twelve spies brought 38 years earlier (Num 13:28). The first generation heard it and refused to enter by faith; now the second generation must face the same obstacles and trust God.  
— Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/  
— Precept Austin: “fortified to heaven” is a hyperbole meaning “well‑defended,” https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-9-commentary

---

## v. 2 — “The people are strong and tall, the descendants of the Anakim … ‘Who can stand up to the sons of Anak?’”

**Traditional reading:** The Anakim were a race of giants (cf. Num 13:33, where the spies said they seemed like grasshoppers beside them). The saying “Who can stand before the children of Anak?” was either a common proverb or the boast of the Anakim themselves. The emphatic “whom thou knowest” points to the report of the spies (two of whom were still alive).  
— Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Gill: the Targum of Jonathan renders this “a people strong and high like the giants,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm

---

## v. 3 — “But understand that today the LORD your God goes across ahead of you as a consuming fire; He will destroy them and subdue them before you. And you will drive them out and annihilate them swiftly.”

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew is very emphatic — a threefold repetition of “He” (He will destroy, He will subdue, He goes before). Israel must “know” (the same verb as v. 2) two things: the greatness of the enemy, and the far greater greatness of God. “Consuming fire” recalls Deut 4:24 and points to the judgment of God on the wicked nations.  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Precept Austin, https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-9-commentary

Guzik notes that “swiftly” does not contradict Deut 7:22 (“little by little”). As far as God’s almighty help was concerned, the destruction could be swift; but for Israel’s own welfare it would happen gradually.  
— Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/  
— Pulpit Commentary likewise: the reference in v. 3 is to the *destruction* of the Canaanites (sudden and overwhelming), while Deut 7:22 refers to the *possession* of the land (gradual), https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/9.htm

---

## v. 4 — “When the LORD your God has driven them out before you, do not say in your heart, ‘Because of my righteousness the LORD has brought me in …’ Rather, the LORD is driving out these nations before you because of their wickedness.”

**Traditional reading:** The temptation to pride begins in the heart before it is spoken. Israel is told that the true reason for the Canaanites’ expulsion is their own wickedness — idolatry, incest and other notorious sins (Lev 18:3, 24‑25).  
— Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Ellicott: “Say not in thine heart, ‘in my righteousness,’ when it is in consequence of their wickedness,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm

Guzik applies this to salvation: believers must never think they have gained right standing before God because of their own righteousness.  
— Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

**Reformed reading (Ligonier):** The chapter is a classic text demonstrating that salvation/possession is by grace alone. God calls His people to remember their sin so that they do not fall into pride and self‑righteousness — the very danger Moses warns against here.  
— Ligonier devotional, https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/call-us-remember

---

## v. 5 — “It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart … but … because of their wickedness … to keep the promise He swore to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

**Traditional reading:** Moses repeats the point, now adding “uprightness of heart” to “righteousness” — neither outward conformity nor inward sincerity qualifies Israel. Two positive reasons are given for the conquest: (1) the wickedness of the Canaanites, and (2) God’s faithfulness to His sworn promise to the patriarchs. Both point away from Israel’s merit entirely.  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Gill: the patriarchal promise is a covenant of grace, not of works, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm

Grant (Plymouth Brethren) stresses that the promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob was unconditional; Israel’s possession of the land therefore rested on God’s faithfulness, not their performance.  
— Grant’s Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-9.html

---

## v. 6 — “Understand, then, that it is not because of your righteousness that the LORD your God is giving you this good land to possess, for you are a stiff‑necked people.”

**Traditional reading:** For the third time Moses hammers home the negative reason. “Stiff‑necked” is a metaphor drawn from a stubborn ox or camel that hardens its neck and refuses the yoke — unwillingness to submit to God’s sovereignty.  
— Ellicott: “the metaphor seems to be taken from a camel … who hardens his neck, and will not bend it for the driver,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Constable: “unresponsive to God’s will,” https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Merrill (quoted by Guzik): “unwillingness to submit to the yoke of God’s sovereignty,” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

Precept Austin summarises the three reasons for the conquest: (1) wickedness of the inhabitants, (2) the surety of the Abrahamic Covenant, and (3) it is a gift from God (grace).  
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-9-commentary

---

## v. 7 — “Remember this, and never forget how you provoked the LORD your God in the wilderness. From the day you left the land of Egypt until you reached this place, you have been rebelling against the LORD.”

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew is abrupt: “Remember — do not forget — how thou hast stirred the indignation of Jehovah.” The rebellion began before they even crossed the Red Sea (Ex 14:11) and was continuous. The purpose of this remembrance is not to discourage but to produce poverty of spirit (Matt 5:3) and destroy any grounds for boasting.  
— Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Gill: “their life was a continued course of rebellion against the Lord,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Enduring Word, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

---

## v. 8 — “At Horeb you provoked the LORD, and He was angry enough to destroy you.”

**Traditional reading:** The “also” (or “even”) singles out Horeb as the most grievous rebellion because it occurred at the very mountain where the Law was given, in the immediate aftermath of hearing God’s voice from the fire.  
— Ellicott: “In the very sight of the mountain of the Law, the Law was flagrantly violated,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html

---

## vv. 9‑11 — Moses’ forty days and forty nights on the mountain; the tablets “inscribed by the finger of God.”

**Traditional reading:** The fact that Moses neither ate nor drank for forty days is not recorded in Exodus for the *first* forty‑day period; Deuteronomy supplies this detail. While Moses fasted in the presence of God, Israel feasted and worshipped the calf. A striking irony: Moses was receiving the tablets of the covenant at the very moment Israel was breaking its terms.  
— Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Precept Austin, https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-9-commentary  
— Gill: “the day the tables were given to Moses the calf was made,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm

“Written with the finger of God” stamps divine authority on the Law and indicates its permanence. The tablets functioned as the “documents” of the covenant, analogous to ancient Near Eastern treaty tablets.  
— Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Thompson (quoted by Guzik), https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

---

## vv. 12‑14 — The LORD tells Moses of the calf and threatens to destroy Israel and make a new nation from Moses.

**Traditional reading:** The Lord distances Himself from the people by calling them “your people, whom you brought out of Egypt” (not “My people”). The offer to make of Moses “a nation mightier and greater than they” was a genuine test of Moses’ heart as mediator. God says “Leave Me alone” (lit. “desist from Me”), implying that Moses’ intercession could — and did — change the outcome.  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Guzik: the offer would still have fulfilled the Abrahamic promise since Moses was Abraham’s descendant, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

---

## vv. 15‑17 — Moses descends, sees the calf, and shatters the tablets.

**Traditional reading:** The mountain was still burning with the glory‑fire of God’s presence even as the people danced around the calf — underscoring the brazenness of the sin. Moses’ breaking of the tablets was not an outburst of uncontrolled temper but a deliberate, public act signifying that the covenant had been broken by Israel’s apostasy.  
— Ellicott: “he deliberately broke the material covenant in the face of the people, who had broken the covenant itself,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Poole (quoted by Guzik): “Not by an unbridled passion, but in zeal for God’s honour, and by direction of God’s Spirit,” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/  
— Gill: the breaking was “an emblem of their breach of them by transgressing them,” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm

---

## vv. 18‑19 — Moses’ second forty‑day fast and intercession.

**Traditional reading:** Moses spent a second forty‑day period on the mountain in fasting and prayer, this time explicitly for intercession (the first forty days had been for receiving the Law). The rare Hebrew word translated “I was afraid” (LXX: *ekphobos*, “exceedingly frightened” or “stricken with terror”) shows how seriously Moses viewed the danger of God’s wrath.  
— Ellicott notes that during the first forty days Joshua was with Moses (receiving the tabernacle pattern); during the second, Moses was alone, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Guzik on *ekphobos*: “exceedingly frightened … stricken with terror,” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

**Charismatic/Pentecostal reading:** Enduring Word (David Guzik) highlights Moses as an intercessor whose prayer “prevailed” and was grounded in God’s character and past faithfulness — an encouragement for believers today to pray with confidence on similar grounds.  
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

---

## v. 20 — “The LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, but at that time I also prayed for Aaron.”

**Traditional reading:** Aaron’s sin was severe (he made the calf and then made a feeble excuse, Ex 32:21‑24). Moses’ special prayer for Aaron is not separately recorded in Exodus but is included in the general intercession there. Jewish commentators linked the later death of Aaron’s two sons (Lev 10:1‑2) partly to God’s lingering anger from this episode.  
— Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Keil & Delitzsch note that Aaron had already been designated for the high priesthood (Ex 28:1), so his survival and later investiture were purely works of grace, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Thompson (quoted by Guzik): “even Israel’s High Priest had to be snatched from judgment,” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

---

## v. 21 — Moses destroys the golden calf.

**Traditional reading:** Moses burned the calf, crushed it, ground it to powder as fine as dust, and cast it into the stream that came down from the mountain — probably the same rock‑stream that supplied Israel with water (Ex 17:6). This served three purposes: to demonstrate the impotence of the idol, to obliterate it completely, and to make the people ingest the consequences of their sin (Ex 32:20 says he made them drink it).  
— Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/  
— Ellicott: “The stream from the rock in Horeb not only gave Israel drink, but bore away their ‘sin’ upon its waters. ‘And that Rock was Christ,’” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm

---

## v. 22 — “You continued to provoke the LORD at Taberah, at Massah, and at Kibroth‑hattaavah.”

**Traditional reading:** Taberah (“burning”) = discontent with God’s guidance, Num 11:1‑3. Massah (“tempted”) = murmuring over lack of water, Ex 17:1‑7. Kibroth‑hattaavah (“graves of craving”) = lusting for meat instead of manna, Num 11:4‑34. Keil & Delitzsch note that the list is not chronological but advances from smaller to more serious guilt — Moses is sharpening the people’s consciences.  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Pulpit Commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Guzik, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

---

## v. 23 — “And when the LORD sent you out from Kadesh‑barnea … ‘Go up and possess the land’ … you rebelled … You neither believed Him nor obeyed Him.”

**Traditional reading:** Kadesh‑barnea was the climactic rebellion (Num 13‑14), where Israel refused to enter the land and sought to return to Egypt. The root problem is identified as unbelief: “you did not believe Him.” Disobedience flowed from unbelief.  
— Guzik: “Israel’s disobedience to God began with unbelief,” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/  
— Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm

---

## v. 24 — “You have been rebelling against the LORD since the day I came to know you.”

**Traditional reading:** Moses summarises the entire history. Ellicott notes the other side of the truth found in Num 23:21 (“He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob”) — Israel is simultaneously rebellious in themselves and accepted through God’s grace.  
— Ellicott, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/9.htm

---

## v. 25 — “So I fell down before the LORD for forty days and forty nights, because the LORD had said He would destroy you.”

**Traditional reading:** Moses returns to the Sinai apostasy to drive home the point: Israel survived only because of his intercession and God’s mercy. The forty days here are the second forty (v. 18), not the first.  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html

---

## vv. 26‑29 — Moses’ intercessory prayer.

**Traditional reading:** The prayer appeals to four grounds:
1. **God’s ownership:** “Your people, Your inheritance, whom You redeemed” — Moses counters God’s “your people” (v. 12) with “Your people.”
2. **The patriarchal covenant:** “Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” — Moses appeals to the unconditional oath.
3. **God’s reputation among the nations:** If God destroys Israel, Egypt will say He was unable or hateful — a concern for the glory of God’s own name.
4. **God’s past redemption:** “Whom You brought out by Your great power and outstretched arm” — what God has begun, He should complete.

— Gill, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm  
— Keil & Delitzsch, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Grant: “Moses’ prayer … was not based on any hope that Israel would improve … but on two great facts, first that God had claimed Israel as His own inheritance … and secondly, on … His unconditional promise,” https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-9.html  
— Guzik calls this “one of the most critical interventions in Israel’s history,” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

**Reformed application (Ligonier):** The intercession of Moses the covenant mediator points forward to Christ, the one mediator (1 Tim 2:5). Even when God’s people have sinned greatly, forgiveness is available through the mediator. Psalm 106:23 recalls this same intercession.  
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/call-us-remember

**Plymouth Brethren / Evangelical (Grant):** Believers today depend on the intercession of the Lord Jesus just as Israel depended on Moses’ intercession.  
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/deuteronomy-9.html

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On this chapter the major Protestant traditions largely agree on the meaning: the land is given by grace, not human merit. The differences lie mainly in application and emphasis:

- **Reformed (Ligonier, monergism.com):** See vv. 4‑6 as a classic proof of salvation by grace alone and total inability — Israel is “stiff‑necked” (totally depraved) and cannot merit anything from God. The intercession of Moses prefigures Christ as the sole mediator.  
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/call-us-remember

- **Lutheran:** Would emphasise the Law/Gospel distinction — the Law given at Horeb was broken even as it was being delivered (Law condemns); the people are saved only through the mediator’s intercession (Gospel). I was unable to retrieve a dedicated LCMS or 1517.org page on this chapter within the search limits.

- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** Wesley’s Notes (available on studylight.org) would stress that even after receiving grace, the people must not boast, and that the record of their sins is meant to humble them and produce ongoing repentance. I was unable to retrieve the specific Wesley page within the search limits.

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik):** Strong emphasis on intercessory prayer as powerful and effective. Moses’ prayer “prevailed” and changed the course of history. Believers are encouraged to pray with the same boldness, grounding requests in God’s character and covenant promises.  
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-9/

- **Baptist:** Older Baptist commentators (Gill) stress that the chapter refutes any notion of justification by works — the doctrinal application is consistently soteriological. Gill repeatedly draws the parallel: “the doctrines of justification by the righteousness of Christ, and not man’s, and of salvation by the grace of God, and not the works of men, are points of knowledge and understanding.”  
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/9.htm
